Zagreb Mirogoj Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Zagreb, Croatia

Not demolished. Zagreb's Jewish community, first present in the 14th century (expelled 1526, restricted to nearby villages until the late 18th century), formally organized in 1806 with just 75 members, growing into one of the Austro-Hungarian Empire's strongest communities. By 1880 the population reached 1,285, divided among Ashkenazi-Neolog, Ashkenazi-Orthodox, and small Sephardic congregations; a grand 1867 Moorish Revival Great Synagogue by architect Franjo Klein anchored community life. Population peaked at 12,000 before the Holocaust, swelled by refugees fleeing Nazi persecution elsewhere. Croatian nationalists demolished the Great Synagogue in 1942, photographing its destruction for propaganda; only 2,214 Jews remained after the war (about 1,200 today). This central cemetery, designed by architect Herman Bollè and opened in 1876 as a multi-faith necropolis, absorbed the Jewish section in 1878, replacing two earlier Zagreb Jewish cemeteries (1811-1877 and 1858-1878) whose monuments were partly relocated here. Chief Rabbi Hosea Jacobi (1841-1925), who led Croatia's Jewish community for 58 years, is buried here. Originally divided into 13 sub-sections (10 Ashkenazi-Neolog, 2 Sephardic, 1 Orthodox) and once holding 4,000-5,000 tombstones, only about 1,500 remained by 2009, partly due to a controversial 1961 Communist-era exhumation of roughly 1,000 graves into a mass grave. A Moses statue by sculptor Antun Augustinčić serves as Holocaust memorial; a 1991 terrorist bombing and a 2020 earthquake both caused damage since repaired.
